title: Non Measurable Sets and the Cost of Choice

items.title: Lebesgue inner measure on the real line
For bounded subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, Lebesgue measurability is equivalent to equality of inner and outer measure
items.strategy: For measurable sets, approximate from outside by open supersets and from inside by closed subsets using the published outer-regularity and Littlewood characterisations, then squeeze the two infima. For the converse, choose compact subsets and open supersets whose measures approach the common value and use the small open excess characterisation to recover measurability.

items.title: Vitali set on $[0,1]$
Assuming choice on the cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$, a Vitali set in $[0,1]$ exists
items.strategy: Consider the partition of $[0,1]$ by intersections of the additive cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$ with $[0,1]$. Each class is nonempty, apply the Axiom of Choice to that family, and record explicitly that the family has cardinality continuum, so this is not a countable-choice argument.

items.title: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, a Vitali set is not Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Enumerate the rationals in $[-1,1]$, translate the Vitali set by those rationals, and use the selector property to show the translates are pairwise disjoint and cover $[0,1]$ while lying inside $[-1,2]$. Translation invariance and countable additivity then rule out both measure zero and positive measure.

items.title: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, no translation-invariant measure on $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$ is both finite and nonzero on $[0,1]$
items.strategy: Run the Vitali argument for an arbitrary measure defined on every subset of $\mathbb{R}$: a selector for the cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $[0,1]$ yields countably many disjoint translates covering $[0,1]$ and contained in a bounded interval, contradicting either nullity or positive finiteness.

items.title: Every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ of positive Lebesgue outer measure contains a nonmeasurable subset
items.strategy: Intersect the given set with the rational translates of a fixed Vitali set. If every such intersection were measurable then each would have measure zero, because its difference set still avoids a neighbourhood of the origin and Steinhaus would fail. Countable subadditivity would then force the original set to have outer measure zero.

items.title: The map $x \mapsto x + c(x)$ is a homeomorphism from $[0,1]$ onto $[0,2]$
items.strategy: Continuity comes from the published continuity of the Cantor function. Strict increase is immediate from the positive contribution of the identity term plus monotonicity of the Cantor function. A continuous bijection from compact $[0,1]$ to Hausdorff $[0,2]$ is then a homeomorphism.

items.title: The homeomorphism $x \mapsto x + c(x)$ sends the Cantor set onto a compact set of Lebesgue measure $1$
items.strategy: Use the gap description of the Cantor function: on every complementary interval of the Cantor set the function is constant, so $x+c(x)$ acts there by translation and preserves interval length. The complement of the Cantor set has measure $1$ inside $[0,1]$, its image therefore has measure $1$ inside $[0,2]$, and the image of the Cantor set is the complementary compact set of measure $1$.

items.title: A continuous image of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ can be nonmeasurable
items.strategy: Take a nonmeasurable subset of the measure-one image of the Cantor set, pull it back through the homeomorphism to a subset of the Cantor set, and use completeness to make that pullback measurable. The same homeomorphism then sends a measurable set to a nonmeasurable one.

items.title: A continuous preimage of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ can be nonmeasurable
items.strategy: Use the same witness as in the preceding corollary, but apply the inverse homeomorphism. The measurable subset of the Cantor set stays measurable while its preimage under the inverse map is the chosen nonmeasurable subset of the measure-one image.

items.title: There is a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is not Borel
items.strategy: Choose a nonmeasurable subset of the measure-one compact image of the Cantor set, and pull it back through the homeomorphism to a subset of the Cantor set; completeness makes that pullback measurable. If the pullback were Borel in $\mathbb{R}$, the subspace-trace theorem would make it Borel in the Cantor set, continuous-preimage closure applied to the inverse homeomorphism would make the chosen image Borel in the compact image, and the same trace theorem would make it Borel in $\mathbb{R}$, contradicting its nonmeasurability.

items.title: Bernstein subset of $\mathbb{R}$
Every nonempty perfect subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has the cardinality of the continuum
items.strategy: Recursively split a nonempty perfect set into nested rational subintervals, always keeping two disjoint perfect pieces, and thereby inject binary sequences into the set. Since the set is already a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, this gives matching injections with the continuum.

items.title: Assuming the real line can be well ordered, a Bernstein set exists
items.strategy: Well order the family of nonempty perfect subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ and the real line itself, then run a transfinite recursion of length continuum. At stage $\alpha$ pick one fresh point from the $\alpha$-th perfect set for the set itself and one fresh point for its complement; the previous theorem guarantees that fewer than continuum many earlier choices cannot exhaust a perfect set.

items.title: Every compact subset of a Bernstein set is countable
items.strategy: A compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed. If such a subset inside a Bernstein set were uncountable, the perfect-set theorem for closed sets would give it a nonempty perfect subset, contradicting the Bernstein condition.

items.title: A Bernstein set has inner measure $0$, and in every nondegenerate interval its intersection has full outer measure
items.strategy: Compact subsets of a Bernstein set are countable, hence null, so the inner measure is zero. For an interval $I$, if the outer measure of $B\cap I$ were smaller than $|I|$, outer regularity would produce an open set missing a closed subset of positive measure inside $I\setminus B$; that closed set would be uncountable and therefore contain a perfect subset, contradiction.

items.title: A Bernstein set is not Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Apply the bounded inner-versus-outer characterisation on a nondegenerate interval. The preceding theorem gives inner measure zero and outer measure equal to the interval length, so the two cannot agree.

items.title: A Lebesgue measurable subset of $[0,1]$ that is invariant under changing finitely many binary digits has measure $0$ or $1$
items.strategy: Every finite binary digit change is, away from the dyadic rationals, a piecewise translation by a dyadic rational, so it preserves Lebesgue measure. Use dyadic intervals to show that the relative measure of the set inside every generation-$n$ dyadic interval is the same, and then approximate an open superset to force that common density to equal the total measure.

items.title: A free ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$, viewed as a subset of $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and hence of $[0,1]$, is not Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: A free ultrafilter is invariant under finite modification, so the preceding zero-one lemma forces any measurable representative to have measure $0$ or $1$. Complementing a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ swaps an ultrafilter with its complement and is measure preserving, so a measurable ultrafilter would also have measure $1/2$, contradiction.

items.title: What the Vitali set, Bernstein sets and free ultrafilters cost in choice

title: Non Measurable Sets and the Cost of Choice — Examples

items.title: The cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ meet $[0,1]$ in pairwise disjoint classes, and rational translates of a Vitali set count them
items.strategy: Work directly with the relation $x-y\in\mathbb Q$. Show that each real of $[0,1]$ differs by a rational in $[-1,1]$ from exactly one point of a Vitali selector, and that distinct rationals give disjoint translates.

items.title: The map $x \mapsto x+c(x)$ carries the Cantor set onto a compact set of Lebesgue measure $1$ inside $[0,2]$
items.strategy: Use the two A-page lemmas and compute the images of a few explicit gaps and Cantor points, so the homeomorphism route behind the measurable-but-not-Borel witness is concrete rather than schematic.

items.title: A Vitali set shows that not every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Use the A-page existence theorem and the nonmeasurability theorem together: the same object exists under choice and contradicts the claim immediately.

items.title: A Bernstein set is dense in every interval, has inner measure $0$, and is not Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Combine the Bernstein-existence theorem with the A-page measure theorem. Density comes from meeting every perfect subset of every nondegenerate closed interval, while the inner and outer measure conclusions are already established on the A page.

items.title: Two disjoint nonmeasurable subsets of $[0,1]$ can have the measurable union $[0,1]$
items.strategy: Take a Vitali set $V\subseteq[0,1]$ and its complement. The sets are disjoint, their union is measurable, and the complement cannot be measurable because otherwise the measurable difference $[0,1]\setminus([0,1]\setminus V)=V$ would be measurable.

items.title: Assuming Choice, a proper subgroup of $(\mathbb{R},+)$ can be nonmeasurable
items.strategy: Fix a Hamel basis and one basis vector. The kernel of the corresponding coefficient map is a proper additive subgroup, its rational translates cover $\mathbb{R}$, and measurable-proper-subgroup rigidity rules out both positive measure and measure zero.

items.title: FALSE: assuming the Axiom of Choice, every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Refute the claim with a Vitali set, and state explicitly that the choice assumption is part of the false statement because ZF + DC behaves differently, as the A-page ledger records.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous image of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Use the measurable subset of the Cantor set constructed on the A page whose image under $x+c(x)$ is nonmeasurable.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous preimage of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Use the inverse homeomorphism from the A page: it pulls a measurable subset of the Cantor set back to the chosen nonmeasurable subset of its positive-measure image.

items.title: FALSE: a dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$ of outer measure zero and a dense subset of full inner measure cannot both meet every open interval
items.strategy: Use the published facts that $mathbb Q$ is dense in $mathbb R$ and Lebesgue null. In any bounded nondegenerate interval its complement is also dense, has full Lebesgue measure there, and is measurable, so the bounded inner-versus-outer criterion makes its inner measure equal to the interval length. Thus $mathbb Q$ and its complement witness coexistence.

items.title: FALSE, relative to an inaccessible cardinal: ZF + DC proves that a nonmeasurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ exists
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the published Solovay and Shelah remarks: relative to an inaccessible cardinal, ZF + DC is compatible with every set of reals being measurable, so DC alone cannot guarantee a nonmeasurable set.
